Prealgebra · Lesson 1.3

Multiplication

Solve this lesson, free →All lessons

Multiplication is how you count without counting one at a time. Nobody finds the number of seats in a stadium by tapping each one. You spot the structure, multiply, and get the total in one step. Multiplication has the same two freedoms as addition, any order and any grouping. It also has one rule of its own, the distributive property, which connects multiplication back to addition.

Problem
A chocolatier packs a gift box with 55 rows of 88 truffles. The box sits sideways in the shop window, so a passer-by sees 88 rows of 55. The chocolatier computes 5×85×8, and the passer-by computes 8×58×5. How many truffles do they each count?
Show the full solution
5 rows of 8 is 8+8+8+8+8=408+8+8+8+8=40, and 8 rows of 5 is also 40.5×8=8×5=40.5×8=8×5=40​.It is one box, and tilting it cannot change the count. Every product is a grid, and a grid counts the same whichever way you sweep it.
Problem
Multiply in the easy order: 5×9×2.5×9×2.
Show a hint
  • Pair the 5 and the 2 to make 10 first!
Show the full solution
Reorder to (5×2)×9=10×9=90(5×2)×9=10×9=90. Find a pair that makes 10 before multiplying anything.
Key idea
Products can be taken in any order and with any grouping, just like sums. So look for pairs of factors with a round product, like 2 × 5 = 10, 4 × 25 = 100, and 8 × 125 = 1000. Reorder to put that pair together, then multiply.
Problem
Partner up: 4×7×25.4×7×25.
Show a hint
  • 4 and 25 are partners, and together they make 100.
Show the full solution
Group the partners: (4×25)×7=100×7=700(4×25)×7=100×7=700.
Problem
Find the friendly pair first: 2×13×5.2×13×5.
Show a hint
  • 2 and 5 make 10.
Show the full solution
Reorder: (2×5)×13=10×13=130(2×5)×13=10×13=130.
Problem
An arena has 22 seating decks. Each deck is divided into 2626 sections, and each section holds 5050 seats. Multiply the three numbers in whatever order is most painless: how many seats does the arena have?
Show a hint
  • Nothing forces you to multiply left to right. Which two of the three factors make a round number together?
Show the full solution
The 2 and the 50 make 100, so pair those first.(2×50)×26=100×26=2600.(2×50)×26=100×26=2600​.Order and grouping are free, so look for a pair that builds a power of ten before multiplying anything.
Problem
Go partner-hunting in 8×73×1258×73×125, entirely in your head.
Show the full solution
8 and 125 are partners.8×125=1000,8×125=1000,so 73×1000=7300073×1000=73000​. Keep the three pairs in mind, 2×5=102×5=10, 4×25=1004×25=100, and 8×125=10008×125=1000, and scan for one before you compute.
Problem
All in your head: 16×125×5.16×125×5.
Show a hint
  • 16=2×816=2×8, and 88 partners with 125125.
Show the full solution
16×125=2×(8×125)=2×1000=200016×125=2×(8×125)=2×1000=2000, then 2000×5=100002000×5=10000.
Problem
Compute 8×625×125.8×625×125.
Show a hint
  • 8 and 125 are partners that make 1000.
Show the full solution
8×125=10008×125=1000, so 1000×625=6250001000×625=625000. Partner-hunting collapses the whole product.
Problem
In your head: 2×17×5×4×25.2×17×5×4×25.
Show a hint
  • Two partner pairs sit in the list.
  • 2×5=102×5=10 and 4×25=1004×25=100.
Show the full solution
Pair them off: (2×5)×(4×25)×17=10×100×17=1000×17=17000(2×5)×(4×25)×17=10×100×17=1000×17=17000.

So far multiplication has only borrowed addition’s tricks. The new rule shows up when the two operations meet in one problem, either when a sum has to be multiplied or when two products share a factor.

Problem
Split the multiply: 6×12.6×12.
Show a hint
  • Think of 12 as 10+210+2.
Show the full solution
6×(10+2)=60+12=726×(10+2)=60+12=72. Breaking a number into easy parts turns one hard multiply into two simple ones.
Problem
Use the bridge: 5×21.5×21.
Show a hint
  • Write 21 as 20+120+1.
Show the full solution
5×(20+1)=100+5=1055×(20+1)=100+5=105.
Problem
A trail crew is building 99 identical fence panels. Each panel needs 2020 long boards and 77 short ones. Count the boards two different ways. First find what one panel uses and multiply by 9. Then count all the long boards and all the short boards separately and add. Both counts should match, so what total do they give?
Show the full solution
One panel uses 20+7=2720+7=27 boards, so nine panels use 9×27=2439×27=243​. Counting by type gives the same total, 9×20=1809×20=180 long boards and 9×7=639×7=63 short ones, which add to 243.9×(20+7)=(9×20)+(9×7).9×(20+7)=(9×20)+(9×7).Multiplying a sum is the same as multiplying each part and adding. That is the distributive property, the bridge between ×× and ++.
Key idea
The distributive property says that multiplying a sum gives the same result as multiplying each part and adding, a(b+c)=ab+aca(b+c)=ab+ac. Read left to right, it rewrites one hard multiplication as two easy ones. Read right to left, it combines two products that share a factor into one.
Problem
Split the awkward factor: 8×43.8×43.
Show a hint
  • 43=40+343=40+3.
Show the full solution
8×(40+3)=320+24=3448×(40+3)=320+24=344.
Problem
The bridge spans subtractions too. Compute 4×9984×998 with nothing written down.
Show a hint
  • 998 is unfriendly, but 1000 is a dream, and 998=1000−2998=1000−2.
Show the full solution
998 is 2 short of 1000, so multiply by 1000 and take the extra back.4×998=4×(1000−2)=4000−8=3992.4×998=4×(1000−2)=4000−8=3992​.Distributing works over subtraction too, which handles any factor sitting just below a round number.
Problem
No pencil: 7×1003.7×1003.
Show a hint
  • 1003=1000+31003=1000+3.
Show the full solution
7×(1000+3)=7000+21=70217×(1000+3)=7000+21=7021. Split across the round number, then add the small piece.
Problem
Now run the bridge in reverse: compute 86×14−76×14.86×14−76×14.
Show a hint
  • Both products contain a 14. Say the expression in words: “eighty-six 14s minus seventy-six 14s leaves …”
Show the full solution
Read it as eighty-six 14s minus seventy-six 14s, which leaves ten 14s.86×14−76×14=(86−76)×14=10×14=140.86×14−76×14=(86−76)×14=10×14=140​.This is the distributive property read right to left. When two products share a factor, subtract the counts and multiply once.
Problem
Collapse it: 53×28+47×28.53×28+47×28.
Show a hint
  • Both products share a 28, so how many 28s in all?
Show the full solution
Read it as fifty-three 28s plus forty-seven 28s, which is one hundred 28s: (53+47)×28=100×28=2800(53+47)×28=100×28=2800.

One case is still open. The last lesson handled negative numbers under addition and subtraction. What happens when a negative number turns up in a multiplication?

Problem
Compute (−5)×3.(−5)×3.
Show a hint
  • One negative factor, so the answer is negative.
Show the full solution
5×3=155×3=15, and one minus sign flips it across zero: −15−15.
Problem
A research submarine descends steadily, changing its height by −8−8 metres every minute. It starts at the surface (height 0) and descends for 55 minutes. Use repeated addition to find its final height, that is, find 5×(−8).5×(−8).
Show the full solution
Five copies of −8−8 stack up.(−8)+(−8)+(−8)+(−8)+(−8)=−40.(−8)+(−8)+(−8)+(−8)+(−8)=−40​.Repeated addition covers a positive count of a negative quantity. A negative count of copies has no meaning yet, and that needs a different tool.

So one strange case remains. What could (−1) × (−8) possibly mean? “Add −8 to itself −1 times” is gibberish. When the old meaning runs out, mathematicians let patterns decide. Study the ladder below.

Problem
The ladder forces (−1)×(−8)=8(−1)×(−8)=8, since any other answer would break the pattern. Extend the ladder one more rung. What must (−2)×(−8)(−2)×(−8) be?
Show the full solution
Each step down the ladder drops the left factor by 1 and raises the product by 8. From (−1)×(−8)=8(−1)×(−8)=8, one more step gives(−2)×(−8)=8+8=16.(−2)×(−8)=8+8=16​.Repeated addition has no meaning here, so the pattern decides, and keeping it unbroken forces negative times negative to land positive.
Key idea
A minus sign still means “take the opposite,” so (−a)b=−(ab)(−a)b=−(ab). One negative factor makes a product negative. A second negative factor flips it back to positive, (−a)(−b)=ab(−a)(−b)=ab.
Problem
Settle the score from Lesson 1.1: compute (−4)×(−6),(−4)×(−6), and know why it is not −24−24.
Show the full solution
Start from 4×6=244×6=24. One minus sign takes the opposite,(−4)×6=−24,(−4)×6=−24,and the second takes it back.(−4)×(−6)=24.(−4)×(−6)=24​.Each negative factor is one flip across zero, so a product is negative only when its negative factors come in an odd count.
Problem
Compute (−2)×(−6).(−2)×(−6).
Show a hint
  • Two negatives cancel, so the answer is positive.
Show the full solution
The two minus signs flip back to positive: 2×6=122×6=12.
Key idea
Each negative factor changes the sign of the product, just as each minus sign did in the last lesson. An odd number of negative factors leaves a product negative, and an even number leaves it positive.So (−2) × 7 = −14, while (−2) × (−7) = 14, and (−1) × (−1) × (−1) = −1.
Problem
Count the signs: (−1)×(−2)×(−5).(−1)×(−2)×(−5).
Show a hint
  • Three negatives, so is that odd or even?
Show the full solution
Three negative factors is an odd count, so the product is negative: 1×2×5=101×2×5=10 gives −10−10.
Problem
Count first, then compute: (−5)×(−7)×(−4).(−5)×(−7)×(−4).
Show a hint
  • Three negative factors, so odd or even?
Show the full solution
An odd count of negatives makes the product negative: 5×7×4=1405×7×4=140, so −140−140.
Problem
Five signs, one decision: (−2)×(−2)×(−2)×(−2)×(−2).(−2)×(−2)×(−2)×(−2)×(−2).
Show a hint
  • Count the minus signs first.
Show the full solution
Five negatives is an odd count, so the product is negative. 2×2×2×2×2=322×2×2×2×2=32, giving −32−32.

These closing problems mix the whole lesson together, finding partners, the distributive property, and the sign rules, all at once.

Problem
Compute (−4)×(−25)×(−1)×(−1).(−4)×(−25)×(−1)×(−1).
Show a hint
  • Count the minus signs. Even or odd?
Show the full solution
Four negative factors is an even count, so the product is positive: 4×25×1×1=1004×25×1×1=100.
Problem
Lesson 1.1 promised you would one day do this in your head: (2025×2030)−(2020×2025).(2025×2030)−(2020×2025). Today is that day.
Show a hint
  • Both giant products share the factor 2025.
  • 2025×20302025×2030 is 2030 copies of 2025, and 2020×20252020×2025 is 2020 copies of it. How many copies survive the subtraction?
Show the full solution
A 2025 sits inside each product, so read it as 2030 copies of 2025 minus 2020 copies, and the subtraction leaves ten copies.2025×(2030−2020)=2025×10=20250.2025×(2030−2020)=2025×10=20250​.When look-alike products are subtracted, factor out what they share instead of multiplying.

Practice these ideas

Practice
Compute 2×87×5.2×87×5.
Show the solution
Partner the 2 with the 5: 2×5=102×5=10, so the product is 87×10=87087×10=870​.
Practice
Compute 4×6×250×5×2.4×6×250×5×2.
Show the solution
Partner-hunt twice: 4×250=10004×250=1000 and 5×2=105×2=10. What remains is 1000×10×6=600001000×10×6=60000​.
Practice
Compute 5×7×5×2×2.5×7×5×2×2.
Show the solution
Pair each 5 with a 2: (5×2)×(5×2)×7=10×10×7=700(5×2)×(5×2)×7=10×10×7=700​.
Practice
Compute 4×25×4×25×4.4×25×4×25×4.
Show the solution
Two pairs of partners, (4×25)×(4×25)=100×100=10000(4×25)×(4×25)=100×100=10000, with one spare 4 left over, so 4×10000=400004×10000=40000​.
Practice
Compute 1×1×487×1×1.1×1×487×1×1.
Show the solution
Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so strip the 1s away and the product is just 487487​. For ××, 1 does what 0 does for ++.
Practice
A licence plate reads 3709437094. Multiply its five digits together, the fast way.
Show the solution
The third digit is a 0, and a single 0 makes the whole product 0, so 3×7×0×9×4=03×7×0×9×4=0​. No other digit matters.
Practice
Compute (61×0×88)+425.(61×0×88)+425.
Show the solution
Resist working out 61×8861×88, since the 0 makes that whole product 0. The sum is 0+425=4250+425=425​. Spotting the zero saves all the work.
Practice
Compute 125+125+125+125+125+125+125+125.125+125+125+125+125+125+125+125.
Show the solution
Eight copies of 125 is 8×1258×125, an old partner pair, so the sum is 10001000​. When a sum repeats a single number, switch to ××.
Practice
Compute 7×1004.7×1004.
Show the solution
Split across the sum: 7×(1000+4)=7000+28=70287×(1000+4)=7000+28=7028​.
Practice
Compute 6×997.6×997.
Show the solution
997=1000−3997=1000−3, so 6×997=6000−18=59826×997=6000−18=5982​.
Practice
Compute 13×9+9×8713×9+9×87, minding where each 9 sits.
Show the solution
One 9 sits to the right of its ××, the other to the left, but order never matters, so both products share the 9: 9×(13+87)=9×100=9009×(13+87)=9×100=900​.
Practice
Compute 23×9+23.23×9+23.
Show the solution
The spare 23 at the end is really 23×123×1. So the sum is 23×(9+1)=23×10=23023×(9+1)=23×10=230​.
Practice
Compute 64×35−54×35.64×35−54×35.
Show the solution
Sixty-four 35s minus fifty-four 35s leaves ten of them: (64−54)×35=10×35=350(64−54)×35=10×35=350​.
Practice
Multiplication distributes over addition, but does it distribute over itself? Test the claim 3×(10×4)=(3×10)×(3×4)3×(10×4)=(3×10)×(3×4) by working out both sides, then enter the right side minus the left side.
Show the solution
The left side is 3×(10×4)=3×40=1203×(10×4)=3×40=120. The right side is (3×10)×(3×4)=30×12=360(3×10)×(3×4)=30×12=360. They differ by 240240​, so the claim is false, and the distributive bridge runs between ×× and ++ only. Tripling a product once is not the same as tripling both of its factors.
Practice
Compute (−6)×7.(−6)×7.
Show the solution
One negative factor means one flip: 6×7=426×7=42, flipped to −42−42​.
Practice
Compute (−9)×(−12).(−9)×(−12).
Show the solution
Two negative factors mean two flips, back to positive: 9×12=1089×12=108​.
Practice
Compute (−1)×(−3)×(−10)(−1)×(−3)×(−10), and count the negative factors before you multiply.
Show the solution
Three negative factors mean three flips, 1×3×10=301×3×10=30 lands on −30−30​. An odd count of negative factors leaves a product negative, and an even count leaves it positive.
Practice
Compute 15×12+15×38+25×12+25×38.15×12+15×38+25×12+25×38.
Show the solution
Collapse in stages: 15×(12+38)=15×5015×(12+38)=15×50, and 25×(12+38)=25×5025×(12+38)=25×50. Then 15×50+25×50=(15+25)×50=40×50=200015×50+25×50=(15+25)×50=40×50=2000​. Four multiplications collapsed into one.
Practice
For thousands of years, everyone multiplied big numbers the same way you do, digit by digit, carrying as you go. In 1956 the great Russian mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov conjectured that nothing fundamentally faster was possible, and in 1960 he said so in his seminar at Moscow State University. In the audience sat a 23-year-old student named Anatoly Karatsuba. Within about a week, he found a genuinely faster method, and humanity had been overlooking a multiplication shortcut for four thousand years. Computers still use his idea today when they multiply enormous numbers, and an even faster method was discovered as recently as 2019. Even the “simplest” operations still hold secrets, and maybe the next shortcut will have your name on it. 🚀
